title: Lessons with W.L. Jackson and learning left-handed
summary: Jackson, a violinist with a music school on State Street, taught him the rudiments but started him off wrong, including playing the trombone left-handed.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: I didn't mind. So I started with Jackson for some time. He was, and by the way, he played the violin. He was a violin player, but he was a wonderful musician, a perfect knowledge of music.
The studio was in the 3100 block on State Street.
I think I've heard of the name Jackson.

He had quite a few good teachers down there. But he himself, he was a terrific musician. But as far as the actual knowledge of the instrument, and later yes I found out that he didn't know. Because there were so many things that he started me off on wrong.
Yeah, all the fine points, yeah.

Yeah, for one thing, I'm left handed by a boy, you know. I didn't know. So, it was awkward for me to hold my trombone with the other hand. I said, well Mr. Jackson, I can hold it and work the slide better with my other hand. So he said, well turn it around. I said, okay, work it. Because of trombone, I mean you can turn it either hand. It don't make a lot of difference, but as you get in later life, it's very awkward. It looks awkward. Yeah. Other than, in reality there's really no difference, but it just looks awkward.
Did you learn it left handed then?
I learned trombone left handed. And it's a very unfortunate thing that I didn't even know that you had to put oil on the slide.
It was a slide, a breeze of sliding anyway, for about eight months.
